facts.text: Validated parameter ranges are the specific values of each input, such as speed, mass, mount height and visibility, between which a model has been checked against physical data; known model limits are documented places where the model is known to be wrong, approximate or silent.
facts.quote: Validated parameter ranges are the specific values of each input (speed, mass, mount height, visibility) between which a model has been checked against physical data, and known model limits are the documented places where it is known to be wrong, approximate or silent.

facts.text: An example set of validated brake-model ranges covers gross mass of 15 to 60 t, grade of 0 to 12%, speed of 5 to 40 km/h, and dry compacted and wet gravel surfaces.
facts.quote: Brake model validated for 15 to 60 t gross mass, 0 to 12% grade, 5 to 40 km/h, dry compacted and wet gravel

facts.text: An example known brake-model limit is that the model does not represent brake fade above 150 degrees C.
facts.quote: Does not represent brake fade above 150 degrees C

facts.text: An example known dust-model limit is validation only above 70% optical transmittance.
facts.quote: dust model validated only above 70% optical transmittance

facts.text: The Chapter 1 phase plan treats validated parameter ranges and known model limits as an evidence deliverable from the sensor-correlation phase.
facts.quote: In Chapter 1's phase plan, the evidence leaving the sensor-correlation phase is literally "validated parameter ranges, known model limits" [Chapter 1].

facts.text: A sensor model's credibility file should record sensor and firmware version; machine and mounting configuration; calibration conditions and conditions held out for validation; reference instrumentation and uncertainty; weather, lighting and material parameters; metric and threshold; error and confidence intervals; known invalid regions; and tuning performed with validation data.
facts.quote: sensor and firmware version; machine and mounting configuration; which conditions were used for calibration and which held out for validation; reference instrumentation and its uncertainty; weather, lighting and material parameters; metric and threshold; error and confidence intervals;

facts.text: Model credibility records should include known discrepancies, including biases, unexplained residuals and non-conservative cases.
facts.quote: Chapter 10 adds known discrepancies (biases, unexplained residuals, non-conservative cases)

facts.text: Model credibility records should include change triggers: product, software or environment changes that invalidate the evidence.
facts.quote: change triggers, the product, software or environment changes that invalidate the evidence [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Known model limits are safety information, and records of ranges and limits prevent a model from being silently extrapolated to a different machine or sensor position.
facts.quote: Known limits are safety information. The failure these records prevent is a model "silently extrapolated to a different machine or sensor position" [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Failed validation cases should remain in model records because deleting them destroys information about model-form weakness.
facts.quote: Failed validation cases belong in the record; deleting them destroys information about model-form weakness [Chapter 10].

facts.text: With 100 or more machine models and many sensor positions, the organization will repeatedly need to determine whether an existing model covers a new case; only written parameter ranges and model limits can answer that question.
facts.quote: With 100 or more machine models and many sensor positions, the organization will constantly ask whether an existing model covers a new case. Only written ranges and limits can answer [Chapter 10].
